instructional_purpose: Teaches marked ordering of the accusative object: placing it ahead of its governing verb for focus or contrast, and leaving it unexpressed when discourse makes it recoverable. Both are framed as options that leave the grammatical role, and therefore the case, untouched.
concepts_taught: preposing the object (تقديم) as a focus device
environments where object-initial order is presented as obligatory rather than stylistic
a pronoun on the verb co-referring with a preposed noun
the detached accusative pronoun series (إيّا) as the only way to prepose a pronominal object
omission (حذف) of a recoverable object
case invariance of the object under reordering
topic-then-comment reading produced by preposing

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The unmarked verbal-clause order is verb, agent, object, and every other order is marked.
An object placed before its verb keeps accusative marking because its role has not changed.
When a pre-verbal noun is echoed by an object pronoun on the verb, the accusative is the only admissible reading.
An interrogative word carrying the object role must stand at the head of its clause.
A pronominal object cannot be preposed as an attached clitic and must be realized with the detached series.
Restriction particles force the restricted object to precede the verb.
A transitive verb with no overt object in a recoverable context has a deleted object rather than an intransitive use.
Preposing signals emphasis on the preposed element.

recognition_criteria: an accusative-marked noun standing in front of the verb that governs it
a verb carrying an object pronoun whose referent is a noun already named earlier in the same clause
a detached accusative pronoun in pre-verbal position
a transitive verb with neither an overt noun object nor an object clitic, with the referent supplied by the previous turn
an interrogative in clause-initial position that answers to the object role
procedures: locate the object, move it to the head of the clause, and leave its accusative marking untouched
attach an object pronoun to the verb matching the gender and number of the preposed noun
select the member of the detached series matching person, gender and number when the object is pronominal
test whether the antecedent is close and unambiguous before leaving the object unexpressed
conditions: free choice of ordering exists only where no obligatory-fronting trigger is present
omission requires an antecedent near enough that no ambiguity arises
the detached form is used only where an attached pronoun cannot be hosted
exceptions: interrogative objects are not free to remain after the verb
pronominal objects fall outside the ordinary preposing procedure and need a separate form
restriction contexts are presented as removing the ordering choice
contrasts: unmarked verb-first order versus object-first order
attached object pronoun versus detached object pronoun
overt object versus unexpressed object
a preposed noun accompanied by a resumptive pronoun versus one that is not

common_mistakes.pattern: preposing a noun object but leaving the verb without any object pronoun
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the lesson treats the emphatic preposing construction as expecting the object slot on the verb to be filled
common_mistakes.correction_principle: pair preposing with a pronoun on the verb that agrees with the preposed noun

common_mistakes.pattern: leaving an interrogative object in its post-verbal position
common_mistakes.why_wrong: interrogatives claim the head of the clause and cannot be governed from in front
common_mistakes.correction_principle: move the interrogative to initial position and leave the rest of the clause intact

common_mistakes.pattern: placing an attached pronoun at the head of the clause
common_mistakes.why_wrong: an attached pronoun has no independent standing and cannot begin a clause
common_mistakes.correction_principle: switch to the detached accusative form when a pronoun must be preposed

common_mistakes.pattern: changing the preposed noun to nominative
common_mistakes.why_wrong: reordering does not reassign the grammatical role, and case follows role
common_mistakes.correction_principle: determine case from role, never from linear position

misleading_shortcuts: reading every clause-initial accusative as emphatic
assuming a resumptive pronoun is required by every instance of preposing
treating an unexpressed object as evidence that the verb is intransitive
inferring case from position rather than from role
worked_analysis_stages: state the unmarked ordering of the clause
state the reordered version
identify which element now carries the object slot on the verb
name the discourse effect the reordering produces
paradigms: the detached accusative pronoun series laid out across person, gender and number
exercise_types: multiple-choice identification of the role of a clause-initial element
multiple-choice discrimination of obligatory from optional preposing
free-response conversion of an unmarked clause into a preposed one with a resumptive pronoun
free-response production of a detached pronoun form
terminology recall for the two process names
prerequisite_knowledge: accusative marking on the direct object
new_knowledge: the distinction between optional and obligatory object preposing
the detached accusative pronoun series and its licensing condition
resumption as an accompaniment of preposing
licensed omission of a recoverable object
later_dependencies: exception and restriction constructions
topic-comment sentence analysis
reconstruction of deleted governors and deleted complements
verbs taking two objects
sarf_relevance: low — only the detached pronoun series carries morphology; the lesson is about ordering, not word formation.
nahw_relevance: high — ordering, retention of case under reordering, resumption and null complements are core governance material.
tutor_drill_relevance: strong for conversion drills between unmarked and preposed order and for choosing detached versus attached pronoun forms; weak for drilling emphasis judgments, which are not decidable from the sentence alone.
rich_hover_relevance: high value: a reader meeting an accusative noun before its verb needs to be told why it is accusative and, when a pronoun follows on the verb, what that pronoun points back to.
corpus_pvn_relevance: particle and pronoun entries for the detached accusative series and for interrogatives used in object role; noun and verb entries are unaffected since no new lexical class is introduced.
required_evidence: per occurrence the governing verb, the linear position of the candidate object, presence or absence of a co-referent pronoun on the verb, and the case mark; a preposing analysis cannot be confirmed without all four.
uncertainty_flags: rival analyses: a pre-verbal noun echoed by a pronoun on the verb belongs to a chapter of the tradition that licenses both accusative and nominative readings, so the lesson's single-case rule is narrower than the received doctrine
school-dependent: the claim that restriction particles force the restricted object forward needs checking against the usual placement of the restricted term at the end
deletion of an object versus objectless use of a transitive verb is an analytic decision, not an observable fact of the string
new_capability_required: co-reference linking between a pre-verbal accusative noun and a later object pronoun, plus recovery of an unexpressed object from prior discourse — neither is expressible in the five capability families with real consumers

instructional_purpose: Introduces the accusative verbal noun that reinforces its own verb, covering its three semantic jobs, its dependence on form-specific verbal-noun patterns, the stand-ins that may occupy its slot, and fixed expressions in which the governing verb goes unsaid.
concepts_taught: the verbal noun of the verb's own root placed in the accusative beside it
reinforcement function with a bare verbal noun
manner or type specification by adding a qualifier or an annexed complement
event-count specification by using a counted form
verbal-noun pattern selection driven by the verb's derived form
stand-ins that may replace the verbal noun in the same slot
set expressions in which the governing verb is suppressed

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A verb may be reinforced by a verbal noun of its own root standing in the accusative.
The bare verbal noun reinforces, the qualified or annexed one specifies manner, and the counted one specifies frequency.
Derived verb forms carry predictable verbal-noun patterns while the base form does not.
A quantifier of totality, a bare quantity word, a synonym verbal noun, or an adjective from the same root may occupy the reinforcing slot.
Fixed accusative interjections and command-like nouns are reinforcing verbal nouns whose governor has been deleted.
A qualifier attached to the verbal noun carries the same accusative marking.
The reinforcing noun must share the verb's root.

recognition_criteria: an indefinite accusative verbal noun immediately after a verb built on the same root
an accusative verbal noun carrying an adjective or an annexed complement after its verb
an accusative counted form built on the verb's verbal noun
a bare accusative verbal noun standing as a whole utterance with no verb present
a quantifier annexed to a verbal noun in place of the verbal noun itself
procedures: identify the verb's derived form
derive the verbal-noun pattern that form requires
place the verbal noun in the accusative directly after the verb
add a qualifier when manner is intended or a counted form when frequency is intended
reconstruct the suppressed verb when only the accusative noun surfaces
conditions: the verbal noun must match the pattern licensed by the verb's form
any qualifier must agree in case
a stand-in must either be annexed to the verbal noun or otherwise point at it
exceptions: stand-ins can replace the verbal noun entirely
the governing verb may be absent in set expressions
base-form verbal-noun shape is lexically stored rather than derivable
contrasts: reinforcing verbal noun versus direct object — the action itself versus the thing acted upon
bare reinforcement versus qualified manner versus counted frequency
unpredictable base-form verbal nouns versus patterned derived-form ones
verbal noun present with its verb versus verbal noun alone with the verb suppressed

common_mistakes.pattern: supplying a verbal noun taken from an unrelated root
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the construction depends on the noun repeating the verb's own root material
common_mistakes.correction_principle: derive the noun from the verb in front of you, not from a semantically similar verb

common_mistakes.pattern: leaving the verbal noun in the nominative
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the slot is an accusative one licensed by the verb
common_mistakes.correction_principle: the reinforcing verbal noun is invariably accusative

common_mistakes.pattern: marking the verbal noun accusative but leaving its qualifier in another case
common_mistakes.why_wrong: a qualifier follows its head in case
common_mistakes.correction_principle: case agreement propagates from the verbal noun to everything qualifying it

common_mistakes.pattern: treating the reinforcing verbal noun as the direct object
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the two answer different questions and one of them is not an entity affected by the action
common_mistakes.correction_principle: ask whether the accusative names the action itself or a separate entity undergoing it

common_mistakes.pattern: pairing a derived-form verb with the base-form verbal noun of its root
common_mistakes.why_wrong: each derived form selects its own verbal-noun pattern
common_mistakes.correction_principle: match the verbal-noun pattern to the verb's form before checking the root

misleading_shortcuts: assuming each verb has exactly one verbal noun
assuming any accusative noun following a verb is its object
assuming derived-form verbal-noun patterns are exceptionless
assuming an accusative verbal noun always reinforces rather than specifies manner or count
worked_analysis_stages: name the verb and its derived form
name the verbal-noun pattern that form licenses
confirm the accusative marking on the noun and on any qualifier
classify the function as reinforcement, manner or count
paradigms: a correspondence table from verb form to verbal-noun pattern spanning the base form and several derived forms
paired lists of frequent base-form verbs with their stored verbal nouns
exercise_types: multiple-choice verbal-noun identification for a given verb
multiple-choice classification of the construction's function
multiple-choice recall of a form-specific verbal-noun pattern
free-response production of the reinforcing noun for a given verb
fill-in completion of the reinforcing slot
prerequisite_knowledge: the notion of a verbal noun
adjective agreement in case and definiteness
reuses_from_earlier: derived verb forms and their shapes
new_knowledge: the syntactic slot in which a verbal noun reinforces its own verb
the three-way split between reinforcement, manner and count
the inventory of stand-ins for the verbal noun
deletion of the governor in fixed expressions
later_dependencies: the accusative of cause, which is distinguished from this construction by root and function
the circumstantial and specification accusatives
reconstruction of suppressed governors
stylistic reading of classical prose and verse
sarf_relevance: high — the construction cannot be produced at all without the correct form-specific verbal-noun pattern.
nahw_relevance: high — an accusative slot licensed by the verb, plus a licensed deletion of the governor.
tutor_drill_relevance: very strong: verbal-noun production keyed to verb form, and function classification among reinforcement, manner and count, are both mechanically checkable drills.
rich_hover_relevance: hover must separate a verbal noun reinforcing its verb from a same-root noun filling some other role, and should surface the understood verb behind a bare accusative interjection.
corpus_pvn_relevance: noun entries for verbal-noun headwords across base and derived patterns, linked to verb entries of the same root; a small closed set of fixed accusative interjections behaves lexically and warrants its own entries.
required_evidence: per occurrence the verb's root and form, the candidate noun's root and pattern, its case mark, and whether a qualifier, annexed complement or count form accompanies it.
uncertainty_flags: analysis-dependent: whether fixed accusative interjections are genuinely this construction with a deleted governor, or lexicalized adverbials, is a choice among analyses
the lesson states root identity as definitional yet its own list of stand-ins includes synonym verbal nouns, which weakens the criterion
base-form verbal-noun patterns are described as merely various, so the pattern table is not complete enough to project automatically

instructional_purpose: Presents the accusative verbal noun that states the motive for an action, the three admissibility conditions it must satisfy, the prepositional paraphrase used when those conditions fail, and the test the lesson offers for telling it apart from the reinforcing verbal noun of the previous lesson.
concepts_taught: a verbal noun in the accusative naming the reason for the action
the requirement that the word be a verbal noun and not any noun
the requirement that its sense be causal
the requirement that agent and time coincide with the main verb
prepositional alternatives available when a condition fails
a semantic family of motive-denoting verbal nouns
a root-based test separating cause from reinforcement

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A verbal noun in the accusative can carry the motive of the action with no preposition present.
Admissibility requires verbal-noun status, causal sense, and shared agent and time with the governing verb.
A definite verbal noun must switch to a prepositional phrase instead of the bare accusative.
Difference of root from the verb is the criterion separating the cause accusative from the reinforcing verbal noun.
When the agent of the motive differs from the agent of the main verb, only the prepositional construction is available.
Motive accusatives form a recognizable semantic class of emotions, desires, fears and social obligations.
The bare accusative is the more eloquent of the two available constructions.

recognition_criteria: an indefinite accusative verbal noun that answers a why-question about the main verb
an accusative verbal noun whose root differs from the verb's root
an accusative verbal noun followed by a preposition introducing the thing desired or feared
an accusative verbal noun in annexation whose head names a motive
procedures: confirm that the candidate is a verbal noun rather than an ordinary noun
confirm that it answers a why-question rather than a how-question
confirm that the one who acts and the one who is motivated are the same, at the same time
if any condition fails, substitute a preposition plus the noun
check root identity against the verb to separate this role from the reinforcing verbal noun
conditions: verbal-noun status is a hard precondition
causal reading is a hard precondition
identity of agent and of time between motive and main verb is a hard precondition
the lesson requires indefiniteness for the bare accusative form
exceptions: a definite motive is expressed prepositionally instead
differing agents force the prepositional construction
the lesson concedes that annexed motive nouns occur in the accusative in classical scripture and calls this acceptable
contrasts: cause accusative versus reinforcing verbal noun — different root and why-question versus same root and how-question
bare accusative versus preposition plus verbal noun
bare accusative versus a for-the-sake-of phrase, which tolerates different agents
a verbal noun as motive versus an ordinary noun, which cannot fill the slot

common_mistakes.pattern: putting a non-derived ordinary noun in the motive slot
common_mistakes.why_wrong: only verbal nouns can carry the causal accusative role
common_mistakes.correction_principle: name the motive with the verbal noun and let a preposition introduce the concrete thing desired

common_mistakes.pattern: using a definite verbal noun in the bare accusative
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the lesson restricts the bare accusative to indefinite motive nouns
common_mistakes.correction_principle: switch to the prepositional construction once the motive noun is made definite

common_mistakes.pattern: using the bare accusative when the motive belongs to someone other than the verb's agent
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the construction presupposes one agent behind both the action and the motive
common_mistakes.correction_principle: when the agents diverge, express the motive prepositionally

common_mistakes.pattern: labelling a motive accusative as a reinforcing verbal noun or the reverse
common_mistakes.why_wrong: both are accusative verbal nouns after a verb, so surface shape does not decide
common_mistakes.correction_principle: compare roots and ask whether the noun states why or states how

common_mistakes.pattern: leaving the motive noun out of the accusative
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the role is an accusative one
common_mistakes.correction_principle: case follows the role, and this role is accusative

misleading_shortcuts: treating any accusative noun after a verb as a motive whenever a causal reading is imaginable
treating root difference alone as sufficient to identify the role
treating definiteness as a single category and overlooking annexation, which the lesson itself shows behaving differently
assuming every prepositional motive phrase could be rewritten as a bare accusative
worked_analysis_stages: quote the verb and the candidate noun in schematic form
check verbal-noun status and name the source verb form
check that agent and time coincide
state the resulting role label
paradigms: a table of frequent motive verbal nouns paired with their source verbs and derived forms
exercise_types: multiple-choice identification of the role of an accusative noun

multiple-choice selection of when a preposition is required

prerequisite_knowledge: verbal nouns and their derivation across verb forms
the reinforcing verbal noun construction from the previous lesson
new_knowledge: a second accusative role filled by a verbal noun, with a causal rather than reinforcing function
an explicit three-condition admissibility test
the prepositional fallback and its triggers
a pairwise discriminator against the reinforcing verbal noun

any downstream role-tagging over accusative nouns

nahw_relevance: high — a distinct accusative role with explicit licensing conditions and a prepositional alternative.
tutor_drill_relevance: strong for condition-checking drills and for forced-choice discrimination between the two verbal-noun accusatives; weaker for production, since motive choice is open-ended.

proposed_new_units.summary: A per-token decision table that separates the accusative roles a bare indefinite noun can fill — reinforcing verbal noun, motive, state and respect-specifier — keyed on root identity with the verb, verbal-noun status, the question the noun answers, and agreement with a preceding definite noun.
proposed_new_units.why_existing_insufficient: the catalog unit covering accusative roles enumerates the roles but supplies no decision procedure, and this module teaches four roles whose surface signature is the same indefinite accusative noun after a verb, so disambiguation cannot be inherited from role enumeration alone

instructional_purpose: Introduces the single-word circumstantial accusative that reports the condition of a participant at the moment the action takes place, its three admissibility conditions, the identification of the participant whose state is described, and its separation from an ordinary attributive adjective.
concepts_taught: an indefinite accusative word naming the condition of a participant during the action
the three conditions: indefinite, accusative, and attached to a definite noun
the participant whose state is reported and how it is located
the state may target the agent or the object, and two states may appear in one clause targeting different participants
agreement of the state word with its holder in gender and number
participles and adjectives as the two productive lexical sources of state words
separation of the state from an attributive adjective

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A state word is indefinite and accusative and reports the condition of a definite participant during the action.
The holder of the state may be the agent or the object, and one clause may carry two state words with different holders.
The state word agrees with its holder in gender and number, including the sound plural endings.
The holder of the state must be definite.
Definiteness is the decisive difference between a state word and an attributive adjective.
The state reports a temporary condition whereas an attributive adjective reports a permanent quality.
Several accusatives cited from scripture and verse are state words.
Asking in what state the participant was is a reliable test for the role.

recognition_criteria: an indefinite accusative participle or adjective standing after a clause whose agent or object is definite
an accusative word whose gender and number match a definite noun elsewhere in the clause rather than the noun beside it
two consecutive indefinite accusatives where each matches a different participant
an accusative word that answers a how-question about the manner or condition of the action
procedures: identify the definite participant whose condition is being reported
select a participle or adjective naming that condition
make it indefinite and accusative
make its gender and number match the holder
when two participants have states, order the state words so each can be matched to its holder
conditions: the state word must be indefinite
the state word must be accusative
the holder must be definite
gender and number agreement with the holder is required
exceptions: the lesson concedes that an indefinite holder occurs but labels it unusual rather than ruling it out
collective nouns take feminine singular agreement even when the referent is plural
broken-plural state words appear where a sound plural might be expected
contrasts: state word versus attributive adjective — indefinite and accusative against agreement in definiteness and case
temporary condition against permanent quality
state of the agent against state of the object
the state, which answers how, against the motive accusative of the previous lesson, which answers why

common_mistakes.pattern: attaching the definite article to the state word
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the role requires an indefinite form, and adding the article turns it into an attribute of the preceding noun
common_mistakes.correction_principle: the state word never carries the article

common_mistakes.pattern: leaving the state word in the nominative after an agent
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the role assigns accusative regardless of the case of the holder
common_mistakes.correction_principle: case comes from the role, not from the holder

common_mistakes.pattern: attaching a state word to an indefinite holder
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the lesson requires a definite holder for the ordinary construction
common_mistakes.correction_principle: make the holder definite or restructure the clause

common_mistakes.pattern: confusing the state with an attributive adjective
common_mistakes.why_wrong: an attribute matches its noun in definiteness and case while a state does not
common_mistakes.correction_principle: check definiteness and case against the noun before assigning either label

common_mistakes.pattern: failing to match the gender or number of the state word to its holder
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the state word inflects for the holder, not for the nearest noun
common_mistakes.correction_principle: locate the holder first, then inflect

misleading_shortcuts: treating every indefinite accusative after a definite noun as a state word
treating the temporary-versus-permanent distinction as decidable from the sentence alone
assuming the nearest noun is always the holder
assuming the single-word state exhausts the construction, when clausal and prepositional states exist and are outside this lesson
worked_analysis_stages: quote the clause in schematic form
name the holder of the state
name the state word
state the agreement features that connect them
paradigms: agreement of the state word across masculine and feminine singular and masculine and feminine plural
a list of frequent active participles usable as state words
a list of frequent adjectives usable as state words
exercise_types: multiple-choice selection of a well-formed state construction from near-miss distractors
multiple-choice identification of the holder
multiple-choice elimination of a non-condition
multiple-choice agreement completion for a plural or feminine holder
free-response naming of the role and its case
fill-in supply of a correctly inflected state word
prerequisite_knowledge: adjective agreement and the attributive construction
reuses_from_earlier: sound plural endings in the accusative
new_knowledge: an accusative role held by an indefinite participle or adjective rather than a verbal noun
the notion of a holder that may be distant from the state word
definiteness as a licensing condition on a noun other than the one being marked
a systematic contrast with the attributive adjective
later_dependencies: the specification accusative, which is separated from this role in the next lesson
clausal and prepositional forms of the state, not covered here

sarf_relevance: medium — the productive lexical sources are participles and adjectives, so participle formation and plural morphology gate production.
nahw_relevance: high — an accusative role licensed at a distance, with an agreement dependency on a participant that is not adjacent.
tutor_drill_relevance: very strong: holder identification and agreement inflection are both mechanically checkable, and the near-miss contrast with the attributive adjective makes good forced-choice items.
rich_hover_relevance: high: a reader meeting an indefinite accusative participle needs to be told which earlier noun it describes, and that link is exactly what is hardest to see.
corpus_pvn_relevance: noun entries for participles and adjectives that recur as state words, with the state usage recorded as a syntactic behaviour rather than a separate lexeme; no new particle entries.

the temporary-versus-permanent gloss is an interpretive heuristic that will misfire on lexically stable participles
scope limitation: only the single-word state is treated, so any projection of these rules to clausal states is unsupported by this lesson

instructional_purpose: Introduces the accusative noun that names the respect in which an otherwise vague statement holds, splits it into a subtype clarifying a measure or quantity word and a subtype clarifying the clause as a whole, and lists the trigger environments in which it is expected.
concepts_taught: an indefinite accusative noun naming the respect in which a statement is true
the entity subtype following measures, quantities and number words
the clause subtype following comparatives and verbs of increase or evaluation
the two admissibility conditions of indefiniteness and accusative case
the trigger inventory: measure words, numbers from eleven to ninety-nine, the interrogative quantifier, elatives, and a small verb class
separation of the respect-specifier from the state word of the previous lesson

linguistic_propositions.proposition: An indefinite accusative noun can name the respect in which an otherwise underspecified predication holds.
The construction divides into one subtype clarifying a preceding quantity expression and one clarifying the clause.
Numbers from eleven to ninety-nine take a singular accusative counted noun.
The interrogative quantifier takes a singular accusative specifier.
An elative takes an accusative specifier naming the dimension of comparison.
A measure word takes a bare accusative specifier.
Definiteness disqualifies a word from the specifier role.
The specifier is distinguished from the state word by whether it names a respect or a condition.
The construction should only be used where something is genuinely ambiguous.

recognition_criteria: an indefinite accusative noun immediately after a measure, quantity or number word
an indefinite accusative noun immediately after an elative
an indefinite accusative noun after a verb of increase, filling or evaluation
an indefinite accusative noun that answers an in-what-respect question rather than an in-what-condition question
procedures: identify the word or clause that is left vague
choose a noun naming the dimension in which the statement holds
leave that noun indefinite and mark it accusative
for a quantity trigger, place the specifier directly after the quantity word
conditions: the specifier must be indefinite
the specifier must be accusative
there must be an identifiable vagueness for it to resolve
exceptions: the lesson's number rule covers only the eleven-to-ninety-nine band and does not state what other number ranges require
the interrogative quantifier is treated in one construction only, without its other governing behaviour
measure phrases are shown only in the bare accusative, without the annexation or partitive alternatives
contrasts: entity subtype against clause subtype
respect-specifier against state word — naming a dimension against naming a condition
indefinite accusative specifier against a definite noun, which cannot fill the role
specifier after an elative against the elative's own comparison complement

common_mistakes.correction_principle: strip the article and use the indefinite accusative

instructional_purpose: Teaches the exclusion construction: its three-part anatomy, the one particle and two nouns that introduce the excluded item, and a case-selection table conditioned on whether the clause is affirmative or negative and whether the set excluded from is stated or left out.
concepts_taught: exclusion of a member from a set as a three-part construction
the excluded item, the set excluded from, and the exclusion word
one exclusion word that is a particle and two that are nouns
case of the excluded item in an affirmative clause with the set stated
the two-way choice available in a negative clause with the set stated
case of the excluded item when the set is not stated
the nominal exclusion words taking their own case and annexing the following noun in the genitive

linguistic_propositions.proposition: An exclusion construction has three parts: the set, the exclusion word, and the excluded item.
In an affirmative clause whose set is stated, the excluded item is accusative.
In a negative clause whose set is stated, the excluded item may be accusative or may copy the case of the set noun as an appositive substitute.
When the set is not stated, the excluded item takes whatever case its own role in the clause assigns.
The two nominal exclusion words themselves carry the case the excluded item would have taken, and the noun after them is genitive as an annexed complement.
One exclusion word is a particle and the other two are nouns.
An example whose set-denoting head is arguably present in the clause is labelled as belonging to the set-omitted type.
The exclusion inventory consists of these three words.

recognition_criteria: an exclusion word standing between a set-denoting expression and a following noun
an accusative noun after the exclusion particle in an affirmative clause
a nominative noun after the exclusion particle in a negated clause with no set expressed
a nominal exclusion word carrying its own case mark with a genitive noun annexed to it
a prepositional phrase rather than a bare noun following the exclusion particle
procedures: locate the set, the exclusion word and the excluded item
determine whether the clause is affirmative or negative
determine whether the set is stated or left out
read the case of the excluded item off the resulting cell of the table
when a nominal exclusion word is used, assign that word the case the excluded item would have taken and put the following noun in the genitive
conditions: the accusative rule for the excluded item holds only when the clause is affirmative and the set is stated
the appositive option arises only in a negative clause with the set stated
role-driven case applies only when the set is left out
the genitive on the noun following a nominal exclusion word is unconditional
exceptions: negation opens a second admissible case where the affirmative allows only one
the nominal exclusion words invert the pattern by inflecting themselves instead of the excluded noun
an excluded item introduced by a preposition is analysed as the prepositional phrase rather than as a bare excluded noun
contrasts: affirmative against negative clause behaviour
set stated against set omitted
the exclusion particle, which does not inflect, against the nominal exclusion words, which do
accusative by exclusion against case inherited by apposition

common_mistakes.pattern: treating the nominal exclusion words as invariable particles
common_mistakes.why_wrong: they are nouns and carry case marks reflecting the role the excluded item would have had
common_mistakes.correction_principle: inflect the nominal exclusion word and leave the noun after it genitive

common_mistakes.pattern: forcing the accusative on the excluded item when the set is not stated
common_mistakes.why_wrong: with the set omitted the excluded item is the only filler of a clause role, so that role assigns its case
common_mistakes.correction_principle: when the set is absent, ignore the exclusion word and assign case from the clause role

common_mistakes.pattern: marking the noun after a nominal exclusion word as accusative
common_mistakes.why_wrong: that noun is an annexed complement
common_mistakes.correction_principle: an annexed complement is genitive regardless of the surrounding construction

common_mistakes.pattern: carrying the affirmative-clause rule over into negative clauses
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the choice between accusative and appositive case exists only under negation
common_mistakes.correction_principle: check clause polarity before consulting the case rule

misleading_shortcuts: assuming the exclusion particle always assigns accusative
assuming the three exclusion words behave alike because they translate alike
assuming the exclusion word inventory is closed at three, when the tradition also treats verb-like exclusion words
assuming that an absent set noun is always genuinely absent rather than recoverable from a negated generic head
worked_analysis_stages: name the set, the exclusion word and the excluded item
classify the clause as affirmative or negative
classify the construction as set-stated or set-omitted
name the case and the reason it is assigned
paradigms: a case-selection table crossing clause polarity with presence or absence of the set
a parallel table for the nominal exclusion words showing their own case in each cell
a three-row inventory of the exclusion words classified as particle or noun
exercise_types: multiple-choice identification of the excluded item
multiple-choice justification of a case assignment
multiple-choice classification of an exclusion word as particle or noun
multiple-choice identification of a set-omitted construction among distractors
free-response translation and role labelling

prerequisite_knowledge: negation of verbal and nominal clauses
diptote nouns and their accusative form
reuses_from_earlier: case marking across all three cases
new_knowledge: a construction in which case is selected by clause polarity rather than by a governor
an optional case alternation licensed only under negation
exclusion words that are nouns and inflect in place of the excluded item
the set-omitted type in which the exclusion word suspends its own case assignment
later_dependencies: restriction and exclusive-focus constructions
reading of legal and doctrinal prose, where exclusion carries the argumentative weight
verb-like exclusion words, not covered here
any downstream case-prediction over clauses containing an exclusion word
sarf_relevance: low — no derivation is taught; the only morphological demand is producing the correct case form, including diptote accusatives on proper names.
nahw_relevance: high — case selection conditioned on polarity and on the presence of an antecedent set, plus an apposition alternative, sits at the centre of governance.
tutor_drill_relevance: very strong: the case-selection table is small, closed and fully mechanical, so forced-choice and fill-in drills can be generated and graded exactly.
rich_hover_relevance: high: a reader meeting an unexpected nominative or genitive after an exclusion word needs the polarity and set-presence reasoning surfaced, since the accusative is the default expectation.
corpus_pvn_relevance: particle entries for the exclusion particle and noun entries for the two nominal exclusion words, each needing usage notes for their own case behaviour; the excluded nouns themselves are ordinary lexical entries.
required_evidence: per occurrence the polarity of the clause, whether a set-denoting antecedent is present, the clause role the excluded item would occupy if the exclusion word were removed, and the case marks actually written.
uncertainty_flags: school-dependent: the negative-clause alternation is presented as a free choice, whereas the tradition records a preference between the two readings that this lesson does not attribute
candidate-requiring-review: an example whose set-denoting head appears in the clause under a generic negation is classed as set-omitted, which conflicts with the lesson's own definition of that type
the inventory is limited to three exclusion words and gives no signal that other exclusion expressions exist
the case behaviour of the second nominal exclusion word is stated only through its annexation and not through its own inflectional class, which is itself disputed

proposed_new_units.summary: A closed case-selection table for exclusion constructions, keyed on clause polarity and on whether the set excluded from is overt, returning accusative, case-by-apposition, or case-by-clause-role for the excluded item, with a parallel row set for the nominal exclusion words and their genitive complement.
proposed_new_units.why_existing_insufficient: the catalog unit for accusative roles assumes the accusative is the outcome, whereas this construction can yield nominative, accusative or genitive from the same exclusion word, and the deciding factors are clause-level polarity and antecedent presence rather than a lexical governor, so neither the accusative-role unit nor the general governance unit encodes the decision
